passages.t: The Servant: a bruised reed he will not break
passages.happening:
‘Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations’ (verse 1).

‘He will not cry out or raise His voice, nor make His voice heard in the streets’ (verse 2). ‘A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice’ (verse 3). He will not grow weak or discouraged until he has set justice on the earth, and the islands will hope in his law (verse 4).

God, who made the heavens and gives breath to all people (verse 5), says: ‘I, the LORD, have called you for a righteous purpose, and I will take hold of your hand. I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations’ (verse 6), ‘to open the eyes of the blind, to bring prisoners out of the dungeon’ (verse 7). God will not give his glory to another or his praise to idols (verse 8). The former things have happened, and now he announces new things before they spring up (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 41 God called Israel his servant. Chapter 42 opens with ‘Here is My Servant’ (verse 1), but the figure described does something Israel has not done: he brings justice to the nations with patience and faithfulness. This is the first of the four passages often called the Servant Songs.

His way is gentle. He does not shout in the streets like a herald or a conqueror. A bruised reed is a stalk already cracked, nearly useless. A smoldering wick is a lamp about to go out. He does not finish them off. He mends them.

His calling reaches beyond Israel: a covenant for the people, a light to the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners. The first hearers, themselves captives in Babylon, would have heard what that meant.

At the end of the chapter the word servant is used again for Israel, a servant who is blind and deaf. The chapter sets the two pictures side by side, and the tension between them drives the chapters that follow.
passages.later: Matthew quotes verses 1 to 4 of Jesus, who healed many and told them not to make him known: ‘A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory’ (Matthew 12:20). Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, calls him ‘a light for revelation to the Gentiles’ (Luke 2:32).
passages.hard:
Who is the Servant in this song?

The chapter never names him, and readers have given four main answers. Many Jewish interpreters, and many modern scholars, identify the Servant with Israel, pointing to 41:8-9 and 49:3, where Israel is called God's servant; the Greek translation even adds the names Jacob and Israel to verse 1. Others see the prophet himself, sent to speak to the nations. Others identify a particular person: suggestions have included Cyrus, who is also said to be called and upheld by God, and figures such as Moses or a king of David's line. Still others read the Servant as the coming Messiah; the Aramaic paraphrase known as the Targum reads verse 1 that way.

Many interpreters, Christian and Jewish, combine these views. The Servant is Israel in its calling, but Israel as it is proves blind and deaf (verses 18 to 25), so the calling narrows to a faithful individual who embodies Israel and fulfills its mission, including a mission to Israel itself (49:5-6). Christians confess that Jesus is that Servant, while recognizing that the song's first readers saw the figure only in outline. These notes set out each reading in its holders' terms.
passages.asks: The Servant does not break the bruised reed or snuff out the smoldering wick. Ask whether you feel like either one today. And ask whether you treat the cracked and fading people around you as he does.

passages.t: A new song, and God like a woman in labor
passages.happening:
‘Sing to the LORD a new song’ (verse 10), his praise from the ends of the earth. Let the sea and the islands, the desert and its towns, the villages of Kedar and the people of Sela sing and shout from the mountaintops (verses 10-12).

‘The LORD goes forth like a mighty one; He stirs up His zeal like a warrior’ (verse 13). God says he has kept silent a long time and held himself back. ‘But now I will groan like a woman in labor; I will at once gasp and pant’ (verse 14). He will dry up mountains and rivers (verse 15). ‘I will lead the blind by a way they did not know; I will guide them on unfamiliar paths. I will turn darkness into light before them and rough places into level ground’ (verse 16).

Those who trust in idols and call molten images their gods will be turned back in shame (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The new song is for the whole earth: sea, islands, desert, and the far villages of Kedar in Arabia and Sela in Edom. The rescue of God's people is news for every nation.

Two pictures of God sit side by side. He goes out like a warrior, and he cries out like a woman in labor. Both speak of the intensity of his action after a long silence. The exiles had felt God's silence for decades. Now, the prophet says, he is about to bring something to birth.

The blind he leads in verse 16 are his own people, who do not know the way home. He does not wait for them to see. He takes them by roads they have never walked and makes the rough places smooth.
passages.later: A psalm sings the same call: ‘Sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth’ (Psalm 96:1). And Isaiah later pictures God's care in the same way: ‘Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb?’ (Isaiah 49:15).
passages.asks: God says he has kept silent a long time and will now cry out like a woman giving birth. Ask whether God's silence in your life might be the quiet before something new. And ask whether you are willing to be led by a road you do not know.

passages.happening:
“Listen, you deaf ones; look, you blind ones, that you may see!” (verse 18). ‘Who is blind but My servant, or deaf like the messenger I am sending?’ (verse 19). Though they see many things, they do not take notice; though their ears are open, they do not hear (verse 20).

The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to make his law great and glorious (verse 21). ‘But this is a people plundered and looted, all trapped in caves or imprisoned in dungeons’ (verse 22), with no one to rescue them.

‘Who gave Jacob up for spoil, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned?’ (verse 24). They would not walk in his ways or obey his law. So he poured out his anger on them, and the fire of battle surrounded them, ‘but they did not understand; it consumed them, but they did not take it to heart’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Now the word servant is used of Israel as it actually is: blind and deaf, given a message for the nations and unable to see or hear it itself.

The exiles were a plundered people, in the prisons and caves of the conqueror. The prophet tells them plainly why. It was not that Babylon's gods were stronger. It was the LORD who gave them up, because they would not walk in his ways. And even then they did not understand.

This is the prophet's word to his own people, said with sorrow, and the next chapter begins with God's promise to redeem them. It is Israel's own Scripture judging Israel's own sin. It is not a key for calling any people's suffering deserved, and it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people.
passages.later: The next words in the book are God's: ‘Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine’ (Isaiah 43:1). A psalm of exile confesses the same: ‘We have sinned like our fathers’ (Psalm 106:6).
passages.asks: Israel was given a message for the world and could not see or hear it. Ask what God has shown you that you have not taken to heart. And ask where your own suffering has taught you nothing, and whether it might still.
